record.title: Study reports correlated post-training hiring decisions can raise modeled systemic exclusion
record.summary: A preprint studies ten base and post-trained language models in a simulated U.S. hiring workflow built from sampled occupational vacancy and career-profile distributions across 76 bachelor-level occupations. The authors report that eight of ten post-trained models became less likely to callback older applicants than their base counterparts, with a median negative shift of 4.7%. They define systemic exclusion as at least nine of ten models assigning callback probability below 0.5; under this measure, the aggregate rate rises from 5.6% for base models to 17.3% after post-training, which the authors attribute mainly to more correlated decisions. These are model outputs on generated profiles, not observed hiring decisions. The data are a snapshot of U.S. online labor markets, demographic signals are simplified, and the study does not identify which post-training stage caused the changes.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors evaluate ten base and post-trained LLMs on simulated hiring decisions using generated vacancies and applicant profiles derived from U.S. labor-market distributions across 76 occupations.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Eight of ten post-trained models show a negative callback-probability shift for older applicants relative to their base versions; the paper reports a median shift of -4.7%.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: With systemic exclusion defined as at least 9 of 10 models assigning callback probability below 0.5, the authors report an estimated rate increase from 5.6% for base models to 17.3% for post-trained models.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_SCOPE_LIMITATION
claims.text: The study uses generated profiles and a shared simulated workflow; it does not measure employers’ actual decisions or identify which post-training stage caused the changes.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the generated-profile experiments or estimates was inspected.
The experiment uses generated profiles and a shared simulated workflow rather than observed deployments or employer decisions.
The exclusion rate depends on 9-of-10 agreement and 0.5 callback thresholds; post-training stages are not separated.

brief.importance_rationale: If replicated in applied settings, correlated model selection can concentrate who receives opportunities, affecting employment evaluation and deployment governance. The result is bounded to sampled synthetic profiles and simulated callbacks, not real hiring outcomes.
limitations: Results are author-reported model callback probabilities, not actual hiring outcomes.
Profiles and vacancies come from a temporary U.S. online labor-data snapshot and are simplified rather than full-text resumes and job descriptions.
Demographic signals are binary and use names and graduation dates, which may carry other socioeconomic cues.
The paper does not isolate the responsible post-training stage.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report an age-callback decline in eight of ten post-trained models (median -4.7%) and a 5.6% to 17.3% rise in their simulated systemic-exclusion rate.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper documents the simulated method and reports model outputs; no applied hiring outcome or independent reproduction is established.
technical.mechanism: Post-trained models make more correlated decisions in the generated applicant task; an agreement threshold then increases the fraction assigned low callback probability by most models.
technical.regime: Ten base/post-trained model pairs in a generated U.S. hiring simulation using sampled vacancy/profile features across 76 bachelor-level occupations.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within-model base-versus-post-trained comparisons and base-model exclusion estimates under the same profiles and threshold.

brief.title: Study reports correlated post-training hiring decisions can raise modeled systemic exclusion
brief.why_it_matters: Evaluations that look at average demographic differences one system at a time can miss the effect of many systems making similar choices. If supported in applied use, correlated selection could increase the number of people consistently screened out.
